  1. One use case is live, used by its target role and measured against a baseline.
  2. Everyone knows which AI tools are approved for which data.
  3. There is a named owner for the platform and for each component.
  4. The next wave is scored, scheduled and reuses what you built.

Common traps to avoid

  • Starting with the hardest, most impressive idea.
  • Connecting AI to everything before curating anything.
  • Treating governance as paperwork for later.
  • Declaring success on usage alone.

An AI Operating System is built the way good operations are built: one standard, measured, owned improvement at a time, each making the next one easier. Start small, build on solid foundations and let the results make the case for the next wave.
takeaways: Days 1–30 discover and map; days 31–60 prioritize and prepare; days 61–90 implement and measure.
Choose a first use case with measured pain, usable data, low risk, a motivated owner and reusable foundations.
At day 90, aim for one live, measured use case, clear rules and owners, and a scored next wave.
steps.apply: Write your own 90-day AI OS plan on one page using the three-phase table. Name the sponsor, the AI OS owner and the first use case, and book the day-30, day-60 and day-90 reviews in your calendar.

check.q: Which choice is most appropriate as the first use case in a 90-day AI OS plan?
opts: A fully autonomous agent that approves all supplier payments
Company-wide demand forecasting with data that has not been audited
An SOP question-and-answer assistant for supervisors, with curated documents, human checking and a measured baseline
Connecting every system before choosing any use case
check.why: A good first use case has measured pain, usable content, low risk with human review, and builds reusable foundations such as the knowledge base and permission model.

labs.title: AI OS maturity self-assessment
labs.intro: Rate your organization on the six building blocks of an AI OS plus people and adoption. The radar chart shows which foundations to strengthen first.

dimensions.name: Unified data layer
dimensions.question: How well can approved tools reach live, reliable data from your ERP, accounting, CRM and key spreadsheets through governed connections?
dimensions.low: Inventory your systems, name a source of truth for customers, items and prices, and build one read-only connection for a priority use case.
dimensions.high: Extend proven connections to new use cases and add write access only with approval steps and logging.

dimensions.name: Company knowledge base
dimensions.question: How curated, current and owned are the SOPs, policies, specs and past work that staff and assistants rely on?
dimensions.low: Sort one high-use folder into current and superseded documents, archive the old ones and give each current document an owner and effective date.
dimensions.high: Set review cycles and access labels for every collection and add user feedback as a trigger for updates.

dimensions.name: Assistants and agents
dimensions.question: How far have you moved from personal chatbot use to role-based assistants with defined tasks, access and escalation rules?
dimensions.low: Write a role card for one assistant in one role and pilot it at draft-only autonomy with two champions.
dimensions.high: Use log and test evidence to raise autonomy for proven routine tasks, one task at a time.

dimensions.name: Workflow automation
dimensions.question: How much routine movement of work between people and systems happens through reliable, monitored automation rather than manual chasing?
dimensions.low: Map one process, remove unnecessary steps, and automate a single trigger-and-action hand-off with a named owner.
dimensions.high: Introduce confidence-based routing so people handle only exceptions, and review exception trends monthly.

dimensions.name: KPI and decision dashboards
dimensions.question: How well do shared dashboards, with agreed definitions, support the weekly and daily decisions your leaders make?
dimensions.low: List your leadership team's key weekly decisions and write a measure dictionary for the five measures that inform them.
dimensions.high: Add exception alerts and AI-drafted commentary that cites figures and is checked before it is shared.

dimensions.name: Governance and security
dimensions.question: How well are access control, data classification, audit trails, human oversight and privacy obligations applied to AI use?
dimensions.low: Issue an acceptable-use policy, classify your data into four classes and require single sign-on for any approved AI tool.
dimensions.high: Run quarterly access reviews, keep permission tests in every test set and review logs on a regular rhythm.

dimensions.name: People and adoption
dimensions.question: How prepared and willing are staff to use AI in their daily work, and how clearly is ownership of the AI OS defined?
dimensions.low: Name a sponsor and an AI OS owner, choose champions in one team and address job and monitoring concerns openly.
dimensions.high: Build AI use into standard work and training for every role and recognize teams that improve the system through feedback.

exam.q: A 30-person firm has staff using four different AI tools. Answers are generic and nobody knows which tools hold client data. What is the best first move toward an AI OS?
opts: Inventory current AI use and data, then plan a connected, governed layer
Ban all AI tools permanently
Buy the tool with the most features for everyone
Ask each person to write longer prompts
exam.why: Discover starts with an inventory of current AI use and data; the fix for scattered tools is a connected, governed layer, not another tool.

exam.q: Which of these is NOT one of the six building blocks of an AI OS?
opts: Company knowledge base
Workflow automation
KPI and decision dashboards
A custom-trained AI model built from scratch
exam.why: The six blocks are the data layer, knowledge base, assistants and agents, automation, dashboards, and governance and security; a custom-trained model is not required.

exam.q: A team skips the Map phase and automates its purchase approval process as it is today, with five approval steps. What risk does this create?
opts: The automation will be too cheap
The model will forget the steps
Unnecessary steps are automated, producing waste faster
Dashboards will refresh too slowly
exam.why: Mapping first lets you remove unnecessary approvals and hand-offs; automating a broken process just speeds up the waste.

exam.q: A distributor needs an assistant that combines ERP order data, CRM history and its returns policy. Its accounting package already offers AI bank reconciliation. Which mix fits best?
opts: Build everything from scratch
Buy the accounting AI feature; compose the assistant from connectors, a knowledge store and a model provider
Use only the accounting package's AI for everything
Wait until one vendor offers everything
exam.why: Buy where a standard task lives in one system; compose where value comes from joining several systems and documents.

exam.q: An office wants to compare a new AI provider with its current one for its proposal assistant. What makes this comparison fair and quick?
opts: Reading each provider's marketing claims
Asking the most senior engineer which one feels better
Running both on the office's own stored test set of real questions and good answers
Choosing the one with the longest feature list
exam.why: Model-agnostic design keeps a company-owned test set, so models are compared on real tasks rather than marketing.

exam.q: In a prioritization session, an easy use case builds nothing reusable, while a moderately harder one builds the ERP connection three others need. Both have similar value. What does the foundation test suggest?
opts: Favour the use case that builds the reusable ERP connection
Always pick the easiest item
Pick neither until the full data layer is complete
Let the vendor decide
exam.why: Reusable foundations lower the effort of later use cases, so they often justify a slightly harder early choice.

exam.q: Which item belongs in the connection layer of the reference architecture?
opts: The customer service assistant's chat window
The ERP itself
The acceptable-use policy
A read-only interface to ERP order status with a named owner
exam.why: The connection layer holds the governed interfaces between systems of record and the rest of the AI OS, each with an owner and defined permissions.

exam.q: A shop wants its dashboard to show trends in late orders over the past year. Which connection method suits this best?
opts: A scheduled sync into a reporting store
A live lookup for every chart on every page view
An event trigger for each order
Copying figures by hand into a slide
exam.why: Scheduled syncs suit dashboards and trend analysis that need heavy queries over historical data.

exam.q: An intake assistant gives confident but outdated answers. The team finds three versions of the same policy in the source folder. What should they do first?
opts: Switch to a different model
Identify the current version, archive the others and add an owner and effective date
Tell staff to ignore the assistant
Add more folders to the search
exam.why: Curation fixes the root cause: only the current, owned version should be searchable.

exam.q: In retrieval-augmented generation, when should documents a user is not allowed to see be removed?
opts: After the answer is shown, if the user complains
Never; the instructions will stop disclosure
Before the model sees them, by filtering retrieved results on access labels
Only during the annual review
exam.why: Permission filtering happens between search and answer, so restricted content never reaches the model for that user.

exam.q: A salesperson's assistant has quietly remembered dozens of customer preferences in its private memory. What is the main problem?
opts: Shared business facts are hidden from colleagues and the system of record, and may include personal information
Memory makes the assistant too fast
Private memory is always required by law
The model will refuse to answer
exam.why: Shared facts belong in the CRM where they are visible and correctable, and stored personal information still carries privacy obligations.

exam.q: A reorder agent has drafted purchase orders for three months, and logs show drafts for stable, low-value items are almost always released unchanged. What is a sensible next step?
opts: Move all items, including new ones, to act-and-report
Remove the buyer's role entirely
Turn off logging to save cost
Move only those stable, low-value items to act-with-approval-rules within a system-enforced limit
exam.why: Autonomy is raised one task at a time on evidence, with limits enforced in the system and exceptions still going to a person.

exam.q: An agent reads supplier emails. One email contains hidden text telling the agent to change the supplier's bank details. What design principle protects against this?
opts: Treat external content as data, not commands, and keep sensitive actions behind human approval
Give the agent broader tools
Let the agent act and report afterwards
Store the email in private memory
exam.why: Instructions hidden in untrusted input are a known risk; sensitive actions such as payment details must stay behind human approval.

exam.q: Which automation pattern best describes 'compare invoice, PO and receipt; approve matches within tolerance; send mismatches to a person'?
opts: Scheduled summary
Trigger and action
Approval chain
Match and except
exam.why: Match and except compares records and routes only the mismatches for human handling.

exam.q: Two managers report different gross margin figures for the same month, one from a dashboard and one from an AI summary. What prevents this recurring?
opts: A larger model
More frequent refreshes
A measure dictionary used by both the dashboard and the assistant
Removing the AI summary
exam.why: Shared definitions and sources ensure dashboards and AI commentary report the same numbers.

exam.q: A junior employee asks the knowledge assistant about a colleague's disciplinary case and receives an answer. Which principle was broken?
opts: The AI let someone see more than they could without it
Model-agnostic design
Thin-slice delivery
Scheduled sync
exam.why: Inherited, role-based permissions should mean the assistant never reveals restricted HR content to someone without access to it.

exam.q: A BC clinic plans to reuse patient intake information for a new AI analysis that patients were never told about. Under fair information principles, what should it do first?
opts: Proceed, since the data is already collected
Check whether the new use fits the purposes identified to patients and whether consent or other steps are needed, seeking privacy advice
Delete all intake data
Move the data into private memory
exam.why: Privacy principles limit use to identified purposes; new uses of personal information need review, and a privacy professional should confirm the specific obligations.

exam.q: Before launching a procedures assistant, a team builds a test set. Which set is most complete?
opts: Only the ten most common questions
Questions written by the vendor
Questions chosen after launch based on complaints
Common, edge, should-refuse and not-in-the-documents cases, with answers written by people who do the work
exam.why: A balanced test set covers everyday questions, exceptions, refusals and gaps, with answers grounded in the work.

exam.q: A use case's estimate assumed 70% of 100 monthly hours would be automated, but review and exceptions mean only about 40% is realized. What should the team do?
opts: Hide the result until it improves
Update the value estimate with actual figures and investigate where review time goes
Stop measuring adoption
Double the build budget immediately
exam.why: Comparing actuals with the estimate at regular points keeps the business case honest and points to process fixes.

exam.q: A company's fifth assistant takes as long to build as its first because it needed new connections, copied documents and a separate security set-up. Which operating-model fix helps most?
opts: Hire a vendor for each assistant
Skip readiness gates to go faster
Remove the AI OS owner role
Apply standard patterns and reuse shared connections, collections and permissions through the AI OS owner and readiness gates
exam.why: Scaling depends on reuse of shared foundations and standard patterns, coordinated by a clear owner.

figures.title: The AI quality loop
figures.caption: Click each stage to see how a test set keeps an assistant accurate as documents, prompts and models change.

stages.label: Build test set
stages.text: Write common, edge, should-refuse and not-in-the-documents cases with answers from people who do the work.

stages.label: Run and score
stages.text: Score each answer for correctness, grounding, completeness, safety and usefulness against a set threshold.

stages.label: Analyse failures
stages.text: Find the root cause: a missing document, poor structure, unclear instructions or a retrieval problem.

stages.label: Fix root cause
stages.text: Improve the documents or instructions first; change the model only if evidence points there.

stages.label: Rerun full set
stages.text: Rerun every test to confirm the fix and catch anything it broke elsewhere.

stages.label: Monitor and add
stages.text: Collect user feedback after go-live and add real failures to the test set.
